composition: Nominal designation Fe30Mn 11Al 1.2C, corresponding to the measured chemistry C 1.20, Mn 29.99, Al 11.08, Fe balance (all in mass %). Fe is the base element; Mn (~30 %) and Al (~11 %) are the principal lightweight alloying additions that lower the mass density (measured 6.58 g/cm³), while C (1.20 %) is the austenite stabilizer and the key element driving κ-carbide precipitation. This composition sits within the C-series Fe30Mn11Al(x)C (0.6–1.5 %C) in which C, Al and increasing Mn all progressively lower density, and in which C and Al are the elements that most strongly promote κ-carbide growth.
conclusions: C-1.2 exemplifies the strength–ductility–toughness trade-off in Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steels: raising C to 1.2 % produces a fully austenitic, coarse-grained, heavily twinned matrix carrying ~20 nm coherent κ-carbides, giving a high yield strength of 936 MPa with good total elongation (65.5 %) but collapsing Charpy impact toughness at −40 °C to only 2.5 J — lower than the 54.7 J and 98.0 J of the 0.6 %C and 1.0 %C grades of the same series. Compared with sibling compositions, strength and toughness are governed by κ-carbide size rather than by grain size, ferrite fraction or twin-boundary fraction, so alloy design should target controlled κ-carbide size; the study concludes that designing low-density steels with high strength and elevated ductility is achievable by tuning κ-carbide size through careful adjustment of chemical composition, and that only three compositions (Fe30Mn6Al1C 354 J, Fe30Mn8Al1C 294 J, Fe30Mn10Al1C 237 J) retained high impact toughness, with Fe30Mn10Al1C offering the best balanced combination (642 MPa YS, 72 % ductility, 247 J at −40 °C, 6.69 g/cm³).
mechanisms: Increasing C content promotes κ-carbide precipitation and coarsening in the solution-treated austenite (κ-carbides coarsen from <1 nm at 0.6 %C to ~20–25 nm at 1.2 %C and ~50–80 nm at 1.5 %C), so C — together with Al — is the key element controlling κ-carbide size, while Mn only weakly refines it.

Because κ-carbides form a coherent interface with the austenite matrix (consistent with the (001)κ || (001)γ orientation relationship seen by SAED), their strengthening contribution follows a particle-shear (shear hardening) model rather than an Orowan mechanism, giving σ_shear ∝ f^1/2 · d_Car^1/2; fitting the yield strength against the square root of κ-carbide size gives a slope of 97.1 MPa/nm^1/2.

The strength of the solution-treated low-density steel is controlled mainly by κ-carbide size rather than by austenite grain size, ferrite volume fraction or twin-boundary fraction: yield strength rises linearly with d_Car^0.5 (R_p0.2 = 478 + 97.1 d_Car^0.5), with the intercept ~478 MPa attributed to solid-solution hardening plus grain-size strengthening.

Particle-shear strengthening remains active for κ-carbides as large as 50 nm — well above the typical ~5 nm critical size for the shearing-to-Orowan transition — so the sheared, coarsened carbides continue to raise yield strength.

Shear deformation accompanying κ-carbide shearing facilitates dislocation glide across the κ-carbide shear planes, which weakens the work-hardening rate; hence larger (coarser) κ-carbides correlate with low work-hardening rate, reduced uniform elongation and reduced capacity for high ductility.

Coarsening of κ-carbides progressively degrades both ductility (total elongation A_5 = 64.5 − 6.445 d_Car^0.5) and impact toughness (Akv at −40 °C falls steeply to near-zero for d_Car^0.5 > 2), so C-1.2's coarse ~20 nm carbides directly explain its low 2.5 J Charpy energy despite high strength.

Austenite grain coarsening in ferrite-free compositions (such as C-1.2, 22.5 μm) arises because the ferrite phase present in low-C/low-Mn grades pins and refines the austenite grains; the amount of ferrite needed is small (30 % ferrite gives 7.3 μm while only 3.3 % ferrite already gives 9.9 μm), so grain size is set mainly by whether any ferrite is present rather than by its volume fraction.

The near-constant values of σ_TS (~1350 MPa) and σ_FS (~2150 MPa) across all compositions, including carbide-free and coarse-carbide steels, cannot be explained by κ-carbide size variation and are ascribed to the alloy's unique microstructural evolution, remaining an open question.
microstructure: After 1050 °C/2 h solution treatment plus water quenching, C-1.2 is fully austenitic — a single FCC (γ) phase with no BCC ferrite, in contrast to the 0.6 %C steel of the same series which retains ~30 vol% ferrite. The austenite is equiaxed with an average grain size of 22.5 ± 1.4 μm (D_FCC-G/T, linear intercept, 15° boundary criterion), coarse compared with the ferrite-containing 0.6 %C steel (7.3 ± 1.2 μm) because ferrite suppresses austenite grain coarsening. The grains contain abundant twin boundaries, with a fractional twin-boundary length f_Tw = 51.8 %. A fine dispersion of κ-carbides is precipitated uniformly within the austenite matrix; for this 1.2 %C condition the resolvable particles average 20 ± 6 nm in diameter (Table 3; see also unmapped note on a text value of ~25 nm). SAED confirms the κ-carbides are coherent with the austenite matrix with orientation relationship (001)κ || (001)γ. The κ-carbide size is part of a coarsening trend across the C series, from <1 nm at 0.6 %C, ~2.0 nm at 1.0 %C, ~20–25 nm at 1.2 %C, to ~50–80 nm at 1.5 %C.
processing: (1) Melting and casting: melted in a high-frequency vacuum induction furnace (50 kg capacity) and cast into an ingot of 150 mm diameter. (2) Homogenization: 1200 °C for 5 h, applied to the cast ingot before hot working. (3) Hot rolling: rolled into 16 mm diameter rods followed by air cooling to room temperature. (4) Terminal step defining this sample (proc_st-1050c-2h-wq): solution treatment at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching; the water-quenched state was used for tensile, Charpy impact, EBSD and TEM characterization. Note the solution temperature was varied across the wider study (1050 or 1100 °C), but this sample corresponds specifically to the 1050 °C/2 h treatment.
properties: Mechanical properties (ambient temperature, initial strain rate 1.1×10⁻³ s⁻¹, round tensile specimens with 25 mm gauge length / 5 mm diameter, axis parallel to the rod axis; tensile data labelled parallel to rod axis): yield strength 936 ± 1 MPa; ultimate tensile strength 1017 ± 4 MPa; uniform elongation 37 ± 2.1 %; total elongation 65.5 ± 4 %. From the true-stress analysis: maximum true stress just before necking σ_TS = 1270 MPa and fracture strength σ_FS = 2226 MPa. Impact toughness: Charpy V-notch energy at −40 °C (Akv-40) = 2.5 ± 0.2 J (V-notch perpendicular to rod axis; average of two specimens). Physical property: measured mass density 6.58 g/cm³ (Archimedes drainage method). Characterization techniques applied to this sample: EBSD (FEG-SEM FEI Quanta 650, 20 kV, 0.5 μm step, Channel 5 post-processing; specimens ground and electro-polished in 7 % Nital) for phase distribution, grain size and twin boundaries; TEM (Tecnai G2 F20 S-TWIN, 200 kV; twin-jet electro-polished foils in 10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol at 20 V and −20 °C) with dark-field imaging along [001]γ and SAED for κ-carbide size, distribution and orientation relationship; uniaxial tensile testing on an MTS machine; Charpy V-notch impact testing on an MTS impact tester (500 J capacity); and Archimedes density measurement.
summary: C-1.2 is a Fe–30Mn–11Al–1.2C (wt%) low-density steel from the C-content series (0.6–1.5 %C) of a systematic study on how C, Mn and Al alloying content control microstructure, density and mechanical properties of Fe–Mn–Al–C steels. The alloy was vacuum-induction melted, homogenized, hot rolled to 16 mm rods, and finally solution treated at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching — the terminal condition in which all characterization was performed. The central question addressed by this sample is how increasing C content (and hence κ-carbide precipitation/coarsening) trades strength against ductility and impact toughness.
unmapped: Discrepancy in κ-carbide size for the 1.2 %C steel: the text states the average κ-carbide diameter for the 1.2 %C steel is about 25 nm, whereas Table 3 reports 20 ± 6 nm for C-1.2; the difference was not reconciled in the paper.
